A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same wildfire-evaluation study, with matching authors, framework, datasets and retained experiments. All main-text and appendix pages were readable, including figures, tables and equations, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original forest-fire simulations, convLSTM evaluations, calibration analyses and Next Day Wildfire Spread results in Sections 4–5 and Appendices C–D.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds cross-stochasticity evaluations, architecture comparisons, model rankings and sample-size analyses in Figure 6, Table 4 and Appendices F and H.

M1.justification: The simulator, micro/macro framework, convLSTM-CA architecture, BCE training and ECE formula remain unchanged. v2 introduces the limited Conv-CA architectural adaptation, which removes Conv-AE's spatial bottleneck (Section 5.1; Appendix D.1).

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic NetLogo forest-fire evolution and the Next Day Wildfire Spread dataset, retaining the forecasting tasks, observational variables and stochasticity levels. Additional combinations of existing training/test levels, architectures and sample counts expand evaluation design within this coverage.

E2.justification: The real-data evaluation expands from one replicated autoencoder to comparisons among Conv-AE, Conv-CA, AR-NCA, SegFormer and U-Net (v2 Table 4). Appendix F also introduces quantitative comparisons involving AR-NCA and multilayer/bottleneck convLSTMs; v1's bottleneck comparison was qualitative.

E3.justification: v2 adds all 25 combinations of five training and five testing S-Levels, extends this design across architectures, and varies evaluation sample counts at timestep 59 (Figure 6; Appendices F and H). Table 3 additionally evaluates ECE within Dice-overlap strata. The original 700/300 simulation split and 10-frame observation/50-frame prediction setup remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 expands v1's limited stochasticity-mismatch demonstration into systematic cross-level and cross-architecture tests of ECE's discrimination. It adds sample-size sensitivity analysis and a real-data model-selection case study. The original mismatch experiment and macro-variance analyses are retained in Appendices G and E.

E5.justification: v2 removes the 95% confidence intervals accompanying Dice-stratified results in v1 Table 3, while retaining the bin supports and existing Monte Carlo/standard-deviation reporting. Figure 16 adds shaded convergence curves without defining their bands; no increase in training runs or seeds is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds cross-level heatmap results, architecture comparisons, convergence results and stratified ECE scores. Table 4 reports U-Net leading AUC-PR at 0.3302 and AR-NCA leading ECE at 0.0012. Table 3 also revises existing results: overall Precision/Recall changes from 0.298/0.404 to 0.346/0.311. These unexplained revisions do not establish performance improvements.

T1.justification: The core equations remain, but v2 Equation 4 explicitly labels E[Var(O|F)] as Var(Z_t), and Section 4.2 identifies Statistic-GT with the joint distribution where v1 Section 4 distinguished marginal from joint evaluation. These alter mathematical characterization without supplying a new derivation. Appendix H contains empirical convergence plots, not proofs.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes statistical fidelity through MSE and ECE as more reliable alternatives. v2 makes fidelity to the stochastic process a distinct central criterion, singles out ECE for assessing learned stochastic interactions, and describes conventional metrics, including proper scoring rules, as insufficient for that criterion. Resolving model-ranking conflicts becomes another claimed contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive ECE limitations concerning sample requirements and weak discrimination between architectures, alongside guidance for choosing metrics according to application priorities. It separates statistical fidelity from process fidelity and removes v1's explicit warning that marginal evaluation overlooks global behavior, materially changing the interpretation and qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendices D.1 and F add specifications for Conv-CA, a two-layer ConvLSTM, bottleneck downsampling factors of two and four, and AR-NCA's LSTM/cellular-attention components. Existing simulator and convLSTM-CA implementation descriptions are retained; there is no substantial expansion of training or resource documentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references for AR-NCA, U-Net, SegFormer, model-ranking conflicts and broader physical-system applications. It replaces the Rufibach Brier-score reference with Stephenson and colleagues. The wildfire, cellular-automata and stochastic-video-prediction surveys remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around two explicit research questions and the new process-fidelity terminology. Section 4 is reorganized, calibration explanations move into the appendix, and the appendices gain an overview and a substantially revised organizational structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds cross-level and architecture heatmaps, convergence plots and a model-ranking table. Table 3 becomes a compact single-column table with ECE. Existing calibration plots are consolidated, macro-variance plots move to the appendix, and appendix prose changes to single-column layout. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: The expanded cross-level and architecture tests, model-selection example and explicit ECE limitations strengthen empirical support. However, v2 removes Table 3's confidence intervals and strengthens process-identification claims while calling the per-pixel Statistic-GT a joint distribution, without resolving the marginal/joint distinction acknowledged in v1. These central validity and uncertainty-reporting concerns coexist with better testing, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
